chapter_title: Events and Error Handling for Pallet Robustness

screens.title: Events and Error Handling for Pallet Robustness
screens.subtitle: Make your pallet transparent, safe, and debuggable with clear events and precise errors.

narration.text: In this chapter we will learn why events and explicit error types are essential to building robust Substrate pallets. Events are the auditable, on-chain signals that tell indexers, UIs, and other pallets what happened during a transaction. Errors are the precise reasons a transaction failed, allowing users and developers to understand and handle exceptional conditions without crashing the runtime. You will see how to declare events using the decl_event! macro, how to emit them with Self::deposit_event, and how to define pallet-specific errors with decl_error!. We will practice the common patterns: using ensure! to guard preconditions, using ok_or to convert option and result values into our errors, and avoiding panics so the chain remains deterministic. A running example will be an auction pallet: you will add AuctionCreated, BidPlaced, and AuctionEnded events, and errors such as AuctionDoesNotExist, BidTooLow, and Overflow. By the end of the lesson you will understand how events provide an auditable trail and how explicit errors improve user feedback and safety. Consider how a block explorer or dApp would react if events were missing, or if errors were generic: you would lose clarity and diagnosability. Ready to explore how to wire events and errors into real dispatchables?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Events give a permanent, queryable record; errors provide precise, recoverable failure reasons. Use both to make pallets transparent and safe.

First, you will understand why events are required to make on-chain actions discoverable and auditable. You will be able to declare event enums using decl_event! and attach typed payloads that indexers and UIs can consume. Second, you will design and implement pallet-specific error types with decl_error!, which give clear failure reasons instead of generic messages. Third, you will practice the guard patterns used in dispatchables, primarily ensure!, require!, and ok_or, so that invalid inputs fail gracefully and state remains consistent. Finally, you will link events and errors inside a real starter: an auction pallet, emitting AuctionCreated, BidPlaced, and AuctionEnded, and returning errors like AuctionDoesNotExist and BidTooLow. Each objective includes a small competency milestone so you can check your work. Together, these objectives move you from reading the runtime A P I to producing pallets that are transparent, debuggable, and safe for users and integrators.

screens.title: What are Events in a Substrate Pallet?
screens.subtitle: Events are auditable logs — they don't change state but record what happened.

narration.text: An event in Substrate is a compact, on-chain record emitted during execution to signal a significant occurrence. Events are not state transitions themselves; they are logs that become part of the block's history and can be subscribed to by off-chain services, block explorers, wallets, and other runtime components. For example, a token transfer pallet emits a Transferred(sender, receiver, amount) event after updating balances. This allows UIs to update without re-executing the runtime. Declaring events uses the decl_event! macro. Inside it you define an Event enum and typed variants so consumers know exactly what data to expect. A common mistake is to omit events for important state changes; that leaves consumers blind. Another misconception is thinking println! is sufficient. println! writes to node logs and is not stored in the chain history and may introduce non-determinism. Events, by contrast, are deterministic and part of the block receipts. In practice you should emit events for creations, transfers, approvals, and other actions clients need to observe. Consider what an indexer needs to show and include those fields in the event payload. A final takeaway: events make your pallet's behavior discoverable and auditable without changing the stored state.

keyIdea.title: Event definition
keyIdea.text: Use decl_event! to declare typed event variants and emit them to provide a permanent, queryable trail.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What are Events?
Definition & Why it matters
  • Events are on-chain logs that record occurrences without changing storage directly.
  • They are deterministic and included in the block's event list for indexers to consume.
  • Emit events for actions that UIs and off-chain services must react to, like transfers and creations.
Concrete example
A transfer dispatchable updates balances and then emits Transferred(sender, receiver, amount) so explorers and wallets show the action.
Common mistake
Relying on off-chain printouts or node logs provides no permanent audit trail and is not deterministic.
Example: declaring events
// Example of declaring events
decl_event! {
    pub enum Event where AccountId = <T as frame_system::Config>::AccountId,
                            Balance = <T as Config>::Balance {
        /// A token was transferred. (from, to, amount)
        Transferred(AccountId, AccountId, Balance),
        /// A new token was minted. (minter, amount)
        Minted(AccountId, Balance),
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Events make state changes discoverable for off-chain tools; always include them for meaningful state transitions.

screens.title: Emitting Events from a Dispatchable
screens.subtitle: Use Self::deposit_event with RawEvent::Variant after successful operations.

narration.text: Emitting an event is the simple final step after your dispatchable has updated storage and validated inputs. The pattern is: declare an Event enum in decl_event!, set type Event = Event inside your module, and then call Self::deposit_event(RawEvent::Variant(fields)) at the end of the logic. This order matters: you should emit events to reflect completed and committed changes, not before side effects occur. In the auction example, create_auction should deposit AuctionCreated with the creator, auction id, item id, starting bid, and end block after inserting storage and incrementing NextAuctionId. For place_bid, deposit BidPlaced(auction_id, bidder, bid_amount) after updating the current bid and storing the bidder. Emitting events for both success and significant lifecycle changes provides a complete audit trail of what happened, allowing a UI to show a new auction or a new winning bid. A common misconception is to rely on emitted events to represent intent rather than completed state; always emit after storage changes succeed. Another tip: include only the fields consumers need; avoid exposing sensitive internals. When writing tests, assert that the expected event is in the emitted events list so your pallet's behavior stays verifiable.

keyIdea.title: Emit after commit
keyIdea.text: Deposit events only after successful state updates to ensure the event matches the committed state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Emitting Events
Pattern
type Event = Event;

// After storage updates
Self::deposit_event(RawEvent::AuctionCreated(sender, auction_id, item_id, starting_bid, end_block));

// After updating bid
Self::deposit_event(RawEvent::BidPlaced(auction_id, bidder, bid_amount));
Emit concise, typed events after successful state changes. Tests should assert events to confirm behavior.
Supporting notes
  • Events are included in the block's receipts and are queryable by external tools.
  • Avoid emitting events before an operation that may later fail.
  • Prefer small payloads: include only fields consumers need to process updates.
Example scenario
When a bid succeeds, the UI can listen for BidPlaced to refresh current bid and bidder without re-fetching entire state.

screens.title: Designing and Declaring Events with decl_event!
screens.subtitle: Choose event names and payloads that provide a complete audit trail.

narration.text: Designing events is a small design task with outsized benefits. Start by listing significant state changes your pallet performs: creation, transfer, approval, closure. For each, decide which fields an off-chain consumer needs to reconstruct the action. For an auction we want AuctionCreated(creator, auction_id, item_id, starting_bid, end_block), BidPlaced(auction_id, bidder, bid_amount), and AuctionEnded(auction_id, winner, final_bid). Then declare them with decl_event! as typed variants so type checking helps keep payloads correct. Remember to import types from frame_system::Config and your pallet Config for aliases like AccountId, Balance, AuctionId. After declaring events, link them via type Event = Event in decl_module!. Emit events using Self::deposit_event(RawEvent::Variant(...)). A common pitfall is overloading events with too much internal state; prefer small payloads that represent the action. Also prefer consistent naming: past-tense for completed actions like AuctionCreated or BidPlaced. Finally, write unit tests that assert events are emitted and contain expected values; test assertions are the most reliable way to ensure your event design matches real usage. This process ensures consumers have a clear, typed view into your pallet's lifecycle. Designing and Declaring Events with decl_event! means design events around what consumers need to know, declare them with decl_event!, and test their emission.. In practical terms, choose event names and payloads that provide a complete audit trail.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design principle
keyIdea.text: Design events around what consumers need to know, declare them with decl_event!, and test their emission.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Designing Events
Step-by-step
  1. List meaningful state transitions you want to record.
  2. Choose minimal, useful payload fields for each event.
  3. Declare the enum with decl_event! and alias types from Config.
  4. Link type Event = Event; and emit with Self::deposit_event.
  5. Write tests that assert event emission and payload contents.
Example event set
AuctionCreated(creator, auction_id, item_id, starting_bid, end_block)
BidPlaced(auction_id, bidder, bid_amount)
AuctionEnded(auction_id, winner, final_bid)
Mnemonic
Think Create → Update → Close for lifecycle events.

screens.title: Events vs println! — Why logging is not enough
screens.subtitle: Understand the practical and deterministic differences

narration.text: A frequent newcomer mistake is using off-chain prints or node logs for debugging and assuming that provides a record. There are four clear reasons why println! is inadequate and events are superior. First, println! writes to local node logs which are not part of the canonical block history; when logs rotate or nodes differ, the information is lost. Second, println! can introduce non-determinism depending on host environment configuration, while event emission is deterministic within the runtime. Third, println! exposes sensitive data in node logs where it may be accessible to operators, whereas events are structured data intended for consumption and can be designed to avoid leaking internals. Fourth, events are programmatically queryable by indexing tools and dApps, enabling automated reactions. Conversely, events are stored with the block so explorers and wallets can subscribe to them reliably. In short, use println! only for local developer debugging off-chain; never rely on it as a substitute for machine-consumable, on-chain events. If you need data visible to UIs and indexers, design and emit events instead. This contrast guides both security and reliability practices in pallets.

keyIdea.title: Practical contrast
keyIdea.text: Use events for on-chain, deterministic, and queryable signaling; use prints only for ephemeral local debugging.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Events vs println!
Why println! is unsuitable
  • No on-chain record: node logs are ephemeral and not part of block receipts.
  • Potential non-determinism tied to the host environment.
  • No easy programmatic access for indexers and dApps.
  • Risk of leaking sensitive data to operator logs.
Why events are superior
  • Persisted with the block, creating an auditable trail.
  • Deterministic emission inside the runtime.
  • Indexed and filterable by off-chain services for real-time UX updates.
Check your understanding
Describe a case where a UI relies on events to update a user's view after a transaction.

screens.title: Custom Errors and decl_error!
screens.subtitle: Make failures meaningful by defining specific error variants.

narration.text: Errors describe why a dispatchable failed. Instead of returning a generic failure message, Substrate lets you define a pallet-specific Error enum via decl_error!. Each variant names a clear failure condition such as InsufficientBalance, Overflow, AuctionDoesNotExist, or NotNftOwner. Those errors are linked to your module by setting type Error = Error in decl_module!. When a check fails, you use macros like ensure!(condition, Error:: ::Variant) to return the specific error. This pattern both documents expected failure modes and provides actionable feedback to users and integrators. A common pitfall is creating overly generic errors like Failed, which offer no guidance about next steps. Another risky practice is calling panic! or expect() inside runtime code — panics can stop block execution and are catastrophic. Instead, return Err(Error:: ::YourVariant) via DispatchResult. Well-designed errors also help automated tests assert failure reasons precisely, making debugging and user support much easier. Finally, map Option and Result values into custom errors with ok_or(Error:: ::Variant) to avoid unwraps and ensure a consistent error handling approach. Custom Errors and decl_error! means use decl_error! to define precise, actionable failure reasons and return them via ensure! and ok_or.. In practical terms, make failures meaningful by defining specific error variants.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Error principle
keyIdea.text: Use decl_error! to define precise, actionable failure reasons and return them via ensure! and ok_or.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Custom Errors
Example declaration
decl_error! {
    pub enum Error for Module<T: Config> {
        AuctionDoesNotExist,
        BidTooLow,
        AuctionAlreadyEnded,
        CannotBidOnOwnAuction,
        Overflow,
    }
}
Best practices
  • Name errors to pinpoint the cause and include no ambiguous variants like Failed.
  • Use ensure! to guard conditions and ok_or to convert Option/Result into errors.
  • Avoid panicking inside runtime code; return DispatchResult::Err instead.
Avoid
Unwraps, expect, and panic inside dispatchables — they are unsafe for the chain.

screens.title: Using ensure!, require!, and ok_or in Dispatchables
screens.subtitle: Guard inputs and convert missing values into explicit errors.

narration.text: Guard macros are the main mechanism to abort dispatchable execution with a clear error. The most common is ensure!(condition, Error:: ::Variant) — it checks a boolean and, when false, returns Err(Error:: ::Variant) immediately. Use ok_or(Error:: ::Variant)? on Option or Result-returning calls to convert a missing value or lower-level error into your pallet's error. require! is similar conceptually but starts from a Result and enforces its success. In an auction pallet place_bid, you should ensure the auction exists, the bidder is not the owner, the new bid is higher than current_bid, and that the auction has not ended. Each check maps to a specific error variant so callers know why the call failed. Also prefer checked arithmetic for increments and balance updates, converting arithmetic failures into an Overflow error using ok_or(Error:: ::Overflow). These patterns keep control flow explicit and make it easy to reason about which conditions produce which failures. Finally, use question-mark after ok_or to propagate the explicit error; avoid unwraps or expect which would panic and potentially disrupt block production. Using ensure!, require!, and ok_or in Dispatchables means use ensure! for booleans, ok_or? for options/results, and return pallet errors rather than panicking.. In practical terms, guard inputs and convert missing values into explicit errors.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Guard rules
keyIdea.text: Use ensure! for booleans, ok_or? for options/results, and return pallet errors rather than panicking.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Guard macros
Pattern examples
// Ensure auction exists
let (owner, item, current_bid, end_block) = <Auctions<T>>::get(auction_id)
    .ok_or(Error::AuctionDoesNotExist)?;

// Prevent bidding on own auction
ensure!(sender != *owner, Error::CannotBidOnOwnAuction);

// Require higher bid
ensure!(bid_amount > current_bid, Error::BidTooLow);

// Checked arithmetic
let new_id = current_id.checked_add(&T::AuctionId::from(1u32)).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
Explanation
  • ok_or converts Option into Err(Error) so you avoid unwraps.
  • ensure short-circuits with a clear error when conditions fail.
  • checked arithmetic prevents unchecked overflows and maps them to Overflow error.
Analogy
Think of ensure! as a gate: it either lets execution continue or returns a specific reason why it's stopped.

screens.title: Checked Arithmetic and the Overflow Error
screens.subtitle: Use checked_add and checked_sub, map failures to Overflow rather than panicking.

narration.text: Arithmetic on balances and identifiers must be treated as fallible in a runtime. Using unchecked addition or subtraction risks overflow or underflow which, if left unchecked, can panic or lead to incorrect state. Substrate provides CheckedAdd and CheckedSub traits; operations return Option so you can map None to a specific Error variant via ok_or(Error:: ::Overflow). For example, when incrementing NextAuctionId or computing new balances after a transfer, prefer checked_add and checked_sub and then handle the None case gracefully. This maps arithmetic failures to a clear error that is returned to the caller and recorded in transaction outcomes, instead of causing a runtime panic. Another benefit is that tests can assert an Overflow error in boundary conditions. A common misconception is that unsigned types never overflow in practice; they can, especially when a malicious or buggy input causes extreme values. The safest pattern is checked arithmetic + ok_or(Error:: ::Overflow) so arithmetic failures are predictable, testable, and do not jeopardize block production. Checked Arithmetic and the Overflow Error means always use checked arithmetic and convert arithmetic failures into overflow errors to preserve runtime stability.. In practical terms, use checked_add and checked_sub, map failures to overflow rather than panicking.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety rule
keyIdea.text: Always use checked arithmetic and convert arithmetic failures into Overflow errors to preserve runtime stability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Checked Arithmetic
Example
let auction_id = <NextAuctionId<T>>::get();
let new_auction_id = auction_id.checked_add(&T::AuctionId::from(1u32))
    .ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
<NextAuctionId<T>>::put(new_auction_id);
Why this matters
  • Prevents unexpected wrap-around and panics in the runtime.
  • Maps arithmetic failure to a clear error variant developers and users can act upon.
  • Allows tests to assert overflow behavior on boundary inputs.

screens.title: Example: Filling place_bid with guards and event emission
screens.subtitle: A concrete code snippet showing safe checks, updates, and an event.

narration.text: This walkthrough uses the auction starter pattern to show the exact checks and the event emission. After ensure_signed, retrieve the auction using ok_or to map a missing auction to AuctionDoesNotExist. Use ensure! to prevent bidding on your own auction and to enforce that the new bid exceeds the current bid. Check the block number with ensure!(current_block ::AuctionAlreadyEnded) to stop late bids. For arithmetic such as updating balances or ids, use checked_add and checked_sub and map failures to Overflow via ok_or. After validation and storage updates — insert the new bid amount into Auctions and update CurrentBidders — emit Self::deposit_event(RawEvent::BidPlaced(auction_id, sender. clone(), bid_amount)); then return Ok(()). This procedure guarantees that errors are explicit, state changes are guarded, arithmetic is safe, and events match committed state. When writing tests, call place_bid with failing preconditions to assert the exact error variant is returned, and with success to assert the BidPlaced event is emitted with correct payloads. That both documents contract behavior and catches regressions early. Example: Filling place_bid with guards and event emission means guard the call, update storage safely with checked arithmetic, then emit a bidplaced event to reflect the committed change.. In practical terms, a concrete code snippet showing safe checks, updates, and an event.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Example code
keyIdea.text: Guard the call, update storage safely with checked arithmetic, then emit a BidPlaced event to reflect the committed change.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › place_bid example
Snippet
let sender = ensure_signed(origin)?;
let (owner, _item, current_bid, end_block) = <Auctions<T>>::get(auction_id)
    .ok_or(Error::AuctionDoesNotExist)?;

ensure!(sender != *owner, Error::CannotBidOnOwnAuction);
ensure!(bid_amount > *current_bid, Error::BidTooLow);
ensure!(frame_system::Module::::block_number() < *end_block, Error::AuctionAlreadyEnded);

<Auctions<T>>::insert(auction_id, (owner.clone(), _item.clone(), bid_amount.clone(), *end_block));
<CurrentBidders<T>>::insert(auction_id, sender.clone());

Self::deposit_event(RawEvent::BidPlaced(auction_id, sender.clone(), bid_amount));
Ok(())
This code shows retrieval via ok_or, guard checks via ensure!, safe storage updates, and a final event emission to confirm the change.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid generic errors, panics, and missing events; prefer explicit returns and tests.

narration.text: When designing events and errors, be mindful of frequent pitfalls. First, overly generic errors like Failed or using panic! inside runtime code are unacceptable: they provide no guidance and can halt block execution. Second, forgetting to emit events for important actions leaves clients and indexers without a way to observe the runtime's behavior. Third, using unchecked arithmetic or unwraps can cause silent vulnerabilities or runtime panics. Best practices include: define descriptive error variants in decl_error!, use ensure! and ok_or to return those variants explicitly, apply checked_add/checked_sub and map None to Overflow, and emit events after successful storage changes. Also, keep event payloads minimal and focused on what consumers need. Finally, write unit tests asserting both success events and failure error variants. Tests are the single best tool to guarantee your pallet behaves as designed. Adopting these practices together makes your pallet auditable, debuggable, and safe for production chains. Common Mistakes and Best Practices means prefer specific errors, safe arithmetic, and consistent event emission; validate behavior with tests.. In practical terms, avoid generic errors, panics, and missing events; prefer explicit returns and tests.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practice rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer specific errors, safe arithmetic, and consistent event emission; validate behavior with tests.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Mistakes & Best Practices
Avoid
  • panic!, unwrap, expect inside dispatchables.
  • Generic errors like "Failed" without context.
  • Forgetting to emit events for important changes.
Prefer
  • Specific error variants and guard macros.
  • Checked arithmetic converted to errors.
  • Events emitted after successful commits.

narration.text: As you finish this chapter, hold three ideas in mind. First, events are the auditable, queryable signals that make state changes visible to off-chain services and UIs; declare them with decl_event! and emit them after successful updates. Second, errors should be specific and informative; use decl_error! to list failure modes and use ensure!, require!, and ok_or to return them cleanly. Third, avoid panics and unchecked arithmetic by using checked_add/checked_sub and mapping None to an Overflow error. Together, these patterns ensure your pallet provides a transparent record of actions while preserving the determinism and stability required by a production blockchain. When you write tests that assert events and errors, you create documentation and safety checks that protect users and maintainers. Keep these concepts as the checklist you run through before merging runtime changes.
